Woolly apple aphid

By Gafar Laiya, Gujarat Bio Organics · Updated 2026-11-25

Woolly apple aphid covers twigs, pruning wounds and roots with white cottony wax. Root colonies make galls that weaken and stunt trees. MM.106 and MM.111 rootstocks resist it; the parasitoid wasp Aphelinus mali controls it naturally; registered insecticides such as imidacloprid or thiamethoxam are used as per label when colonies are heavy (SKUAST-K).

Signs

  • White woolly tufts on twigs, cracks and pruning wounds.
  • Knotty galls on roots; trees stunted and weak.
  • Sticky honeydew and black sooty mould.

Control

  1. Plant on resistant rootstocks: MM.106 or MM.111.
  2. Protect natural enemies, especially Aphelinus mali: avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum sprays.
  3. Where colonies are heavy, spray imidacloprid or thiamethoxam as per label; treat root colonies as per your state schedule.

Pesticide safety: Use only pesticides registered for apple by CIB&RC, at the dose and waiting period on the label, and follow your state's current spray schedule (SKUAST-K, Dr. YSP UHF or the state horticulture department).

Questions farmers ask

What is the white cotton on my apple tree?

Woolly apple aphid, a pest that covers twigs and roots with white wax.

Which rootstocks resist woolly aphid?

MM.106 and MM.111.
